Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement

Global Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines offer significant speed and scalability advantages over incremental approaches. However, they historically suffer from lower reconstruction accuracy, primarily due to the fragility of **translation averaging**. This process—estimating global camera positions from pairwise relative translations—is mathematically difficult because relative translations lack scale and are highly susceptible to noise. The presence of "outlier edges" (incorrect relative translation estimates) in the pose graph frequently causes catastrophic failures in the final 3D reconstruction. Existing filtering methods, which often rely on hand-crafted geometric heuristics or random projections (e.g., 1DSfM), struggle to distinguish between noisy inliers and true outliers in complex scenarios, limiting the reliability of global SfM.

## Core Hypothesis

We hypothesize that the validity of a relative translation edge is best determined not in isolation, but by analyzing its consistency within the local graph structure and visual context.

Our core technical insight is to reformulate the **edge filtering** problem in the original pose graph as a **vertex classification** problem in the **dual graph (Line Graph)**. By converting edges into nodes, we can leverage Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to learn complex structural dependencies. We believe that a learning-based approach, which combines geometric data with deep visual image embeddings, can identify and prune outlier edges far more effectively than purely geometric constraints, thereby stabilizing translation averaging.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose a data-driven pipeline designed to sanitize the pose graph before the translation averaging stage. The methodology consists of three logical phases:

**1. Dual Graph Transformation (The Line Graph)**
Instead of analyzing the Pose Graph (where nodes are cameras and edges are relative poses), we will construct its **Line Graph**.
*   In this new representation, every *vertex* represents a relative pose (an edge from the original graph).
*   *Edges* in this new graph connect relative poses if they share a common camera in the original view.
This transformation allows us to apply standard node-classification techniques to the problem of edge filtering.

**2. Feature Enrichment and Classification**
We will assign a feature vector to every node in the Line Graph (which corresponds to a relative pose). This vector will concatenate:
*   **Geometric Context:** The estimated relative rotation and translation.
*   **Visual Context:** Deep image embeddings (e.g., from a Vision Transformer like DINO) extracted from the viewing cameras.
We will then employ a **Transformer-based Graph Neural Network** to propagate information across this graph. The network will utilize self-attention mechanisms to weigh the influence of neighbors, ultimately outputting a binary probability (Inlier vs. Outlier) for each relative translation.

**3. Scalable Graph Clustering**
A known limitation of Line Graphs is that their size grows quadratically with the degree of the original nodes, leading to potential memory overflows on large SfM datasets. To address this, we will implement a **Graph Clustering** strategy.
*   We will partition the original Pose Graph into manageable, overlapping subgraphs based on connectivity.
*   The Line Graph transformation and GNN inference will be performed on these subgraphs independently.
*   Final edge labels will be determined via a voting mechanism where subgraphs overlap, ensuring the method scales to arbitrarily large reconstructions without hardware bottlenecks.

## Expected Contribution

*   **Theoretical Novelty:** A reformulation of SfM outlier rejection as a binary classification task on Line Graphs, allowing the direct application of node-centric Deep Learning techniques to geometric edge verification.
*   **Robustness:** A mechanism to significantly reduce the influence of noise in translation averaging, leading to more accurate global camera positioning.
*   **Scalability:** A clustering-based inference strategy that resolves the memory explosion typically associated with Line Graph representations, making the solution viable for large-scale, real-world 3D reconstruction tasks.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We designed and executed a comprehensive evaluation of a novel outlier edge filtering method for global Structure-from-Motion (SfM). The core approach involved converting pose graphs to line graphs and utilizing a Transformer-based Graph Neural Network (GNN) for binary classification of edges (inliers vs. outliers).

### Datasets
We utilized three datasets with varying characteristics to evaluate performance:
*   **1DSfM Dataset:** Included 15 landmark scenes with internet-sourced photos.
    *   **Reference:** We generated new reference reconstructions using COLMAP to replace outdated Bundler reconstructions. We robustly aligned reconstructions to this reference.
    *   **Metric:** Errors reported in meters.
*   **PhotoTourism Dataset:** Scenes based on the CVPR Image Matching Challenge 2020.
    *   **Characteristics:** Non-metric; position errors are unitless.
    *   **Training Data:** Scene "Piazza San Marco" (249 images, 10,295 edges).
    *   **Validation Data:** Scene "Taj Mahal".
*   **ScanNet Dataset:** 1,613 monocular sequences with ground truth poses and metric depth.
    *   **Subset:** We utilized six specific sequences (0000, 0059, 0106, 0169, 0181, 0207).
    *   **Metric:** Errors reported in meters.

### Implementation Details
*   **Integration:** The method was incorporated into two open-source libraries: **GLOMAP** and **Theia**.
*   **Pose Estimation:** Relative pose estimation performed using LO-RANSAC.
*   **Rotation Averaging:** Performed using robust methods (e.g., L1-rotation averaging or similar robust frameworks standard in Theia/GLOMAP).
*   **Clustering:** To handle memory constraints on large graphs, we partitioned the pose graph into $k$ clusters, minimizing inter-cluster edge cuts where edge weights equaled the number of RANSAC inliers.
*   **Network Architecture:**
    *   Three `TransformerConv` layers with ReLU activations and dropout (probability 0.3).
    *   Total parameters: 35,992.
    *   Input Features: Concatenated vector (393 dimensions) of the 3D global orientation and a 384-dimensional DINOv2 image embedding.
*   **Training Hyperparameters:**
    *   Epochs: 300
    *   Learning Rate: 0.009
    *   Optimizer: Adam
    *   Loss Function: Binary Cross Entropy Loss
    *   Weight Decay: $5 \times 10^{-4}$
    *   Label Generation: Edges were labeled outliers if error > 20 degrees (Theia) or > 10 degrees (GLOMAP) relative to ground truth.

### Evaluation Metrics
*   **Mean Position Error:** Measured in meters (1DSfM, ScanNet) or unitless (PhotoTourism).
*   **Position Recall:** The percentage of cameras reconstructed within a specific error threshold.
    *   **1DSfM Threshold:** 10 meters.
    *   **PhotoTourism Threshold:** 5 (unitless).
    *   **ScanNet Threshold:** 1 meter.

### Baselines Compared
We compared the proposed method against the following strategies:
1.  **w/o Filter:** Translation averaging without filtering.
2.  **MSAC score:** Weighting based on Sampson error (threshold score < 30 removed).
3.  **1DSfM:** Filter based on 1D subspace projections.
4.  **Triangle:** Filter targeting degenerate triplet configurations.
5.  **CleanNet:** Outlier detection network from the NeuRoRA framework.
6.  **Oracle:** An ideal filter removing all translations with errors exceeding specific thresholds ($20^\circ$ for Theia, $10^\circ$ for GLOMAP).

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Line Graph Representation:** We observed that converting the pose graph to a line graph allowed the system to leverage image context (via DINOv2 embeddings) to identify outlier edges, as two images connected in the graph should share similar high-level features.
*   **Performance on 1DSfM:** The proposed filtering reduced the average position error by approximately a factor of 5 compared to the standard 1DSfM filter and improved the recall rate by approximately 6%.
*   **Performance on PhotoTourism:** The proposed method, when combined with the Triangle filter, outperformed all baselines in all accuracy metrics. The standalone proposed method typically secured best or second-best results.
*   **Performance on ScanNet:** Standard 1DSfM filtering decreased accuracy compared to "no filter" on average. The proposed method improved performance across all metrics compared to the unfiltered approach.
*   **Combination with Triangle Filter:** We found that our method and the Triangle filter are complementary; our method removes outlier edges, while the Triangle filter handles degenerate configurations. The combination consistently achieved the lowest mean errors and highest recalls.
*   **Runtime:** The average runtime was 8.6 minutes on PhotoTourism, 2.55 minutes on 1DSfM, and 4.42 minutes on ScanNet. While slower than 1DSfM (which takes seconds), this duration was deemed negligible relative to the total SfM pipeline time (e.g., COLMAP reconstruction took 886 minutes on average for 1DSfM scenes).
*   **Ablation - Clustering:** Running inference on the entire graph without clustering (Ours inference w/o clustering) resulted in lower recall and higher mean error compared to the clustering approach. This suggests clustering improves accuracy by focusing on local subgraphs.
*   **Ablation - Image Features:** Removing image features ("Ours w/o image features") degraded performance compared to the full model, but still improved mean position error over the 1DSfM baseline.
*   **Camera Retention:** The combination of the proposed method and the Triangle filter retained fewer cameras than the Oracle filter. This occurred because Oracle only removes outliers, whereas the Triangle filter also discards degenerate edges which degrade translation averaging despite not being outliers in the strict sense.
*   **Oracle Limitations:** The Oracle filter (upper bound for outliers) did not always lead to the best reconstructions because it does not remove degenerate configurations, and the fixed angular threshold used for the Oracle might not be optimal for every scene.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.

references.name: raw_materials/idea_dense.md
references.text:
## Problem Statement
Global Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines offer significant speed advantages over incremental methods but suffer from reduced accuracy, primarily due to the fragility of **translation averaging**. While rotation averaging is relatively robust, estimating global camera positions from pairwise relative translations is ill-posed and highly sensitive to noise.

The core difficulty stems from the absence of known translation scales in pairwise epipolar geometry; the system must distinguish between short and long baselines based solely on angular measurements. Consequently, "short" translation edges often become outliers that catastrophically degrade the global optimization. Existing filtering mechanisms (such as 1DSfM) rely on geometric consistencies that often fail in complex scenarios or merely remove degenerate configurations without addressing specific outlier measurements. We require a robust, learning-based method to identify and prune these outlier edges from the pose graph *before* the translation averaging step.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that the problem of **edge filtering** in a pose graph is structurally equivalent to **vertex classification** in its dual representation, the **line graph**.

Our hypothesis is that by transforming the SfM pose graph into a line graph—where original edges become nodes—we can leverage Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to explicitly classify relative translation estimates as inliers or outliers. By enriching these nodes with both geometric data (global orientations) and semantic context (visual features from a Vision Transformer), a Transformer-based GNN architecture will effectively learn the local and global structural dependencies required to filter outliers. Furthermore, we hypothesize that the inherent memory scalability issues of line graphs can be solved via a graph clustering and majority-voting scheme.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

### 1. Pose Graph and Line Graph Formulation
We begin with a pose graph $\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})$, where $\mathcal{V}$ represents the set of images and $\mathcal{E}$ represents the estimated relative poses. We assume rotation averaging has been performed, yielding known global rotations $\mathbf{R}_v$ for all $v \in \mathcal{V}$. The inputs to our system are the relative translations $T(v_i, v_j) = (\mathbf{R}_{ij}, \mathbf{t}_{ij})$, where $\mathbf{t}_{ij}$ is a unit-length vector.

To stabilize the learning process, we will convert $\mathcal{G}$ into its line graph $L(\mathcal{G}) = (\mathcal{V}_L, \mathcal{E}_L)$.
*   **Vertices:** Each vertex $v_{ij} \in \mathcal{V}_L$ corresponds to an edge $(v_i, v_j) \in \mathcal{E}$ in the original graph.
*   **Edges:** Two vertices $v_{ij}$ and $v_{kl}$ in the line graph are connected if their corresponding edges in the original graph share a common vertex. Mathematically:
    $$ \mathcal{E}_L = \{ (v_{ij}, v_{kl}) \mid (v_i = v_k \lor v_j = v_l) \land (v_i, v_j), (v_k, v_l) \in \mathcal{E} \} $$

### 2. Feature Embedding
We will assign a concatenated feature vector to each node in the line graph (which represents a relative pose). For a connection involving a shared node $v_j$ in the original graph, the feature vector combines geometric and semantic information:
1.  **Geometric Context:** The global orientation $\mathbf{R}_{v_j}$ of the shared camera.
2.  **Semantic Context:** An image embedding $\mathbf{d}_{v_j}$ extracted using a pre-trained **DINOv2** model (dimension 384).

The resulting input feature vector for each node in the line graph will have a dimension of 393 (384 for the visual embedding plus 9 for the rotation matrix components).

### 3. Transformer-based Network Architecture
We will implement a Graph Neural Network consisting of three **TransformerConv** layers. This architecture integrates a self-attention mechanism into the graph convolution operation.

**Node Update Mechanism:**
For a node $i$ (in the line graph), the updated representation $x'_i$ is computed by aggregating information from neighbors $j \in \mathcal{N}(i)$ and edge attributes $e_{ij}$. The update rule is defined as:
$$ x'_i = W_1 x_i + \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \alpha_{ij} (W_2 x_j + W_5 e_{ij}) $$
where $W_1, W_2, W_5$ are learnable weight matrices.

**Attention Mechanism:**
The attention coefficients $\alpha_{ij}$ are computed using a scaled dot-product attention utilizing queries, keys, and values. We explicitly incorporate edge attributes into the key generation:
$$ \alpha_{ij} = \mathrm{softmax} \left( \frac{(W_3 x_i)^\top (W_4 x_j + W_5 e_{ij})}{\sqrt{d}} \right) $$
where $W_3, W_4$ are weight matrices and $d$ is the dimensionality of the hidden channels.

**Gated Residual Connection:**
To prevent over-smoothing in the final layer, we will employ a learned gating parameter $\beta_i$:
$$ x'_i = \beta_i W_1 x_i + (1 - \beta_i) m_i $$
Here, $m_i$ represents the aggregated message $\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \alpha_{ij} (W_2 x_j + W_5 e_{ij})$. The gate $\beta_i$ is computed via a sigmoid function acting on the concatenation of the transformed self-feature, the message, and their difference:
$$ \beta_i = \mathrm{sigmoid} \left( W_6^\top [W_1 x_i, m_i, W_1 x_i - m_i] \right) $$

The network will output a binary classification (Inlier/Outlier) for each node in $L(\mathcal{G})$, which corresponds to an edge in $\mathcal{G}$.

### 4. Scalability via Graph Clustering
Converting a dense pose graph to a line graph results in a quadratic expansion of edges ($|\mathcal{E}_L| \approx \frac{1}{2}\sum \deg(v)^2$), causing memory overflows. To handle arbitrarily large SfM graphs, we will implement a divide-and-conquer strategy:

1.  **Partitioning:** We will partition $\mathcal{G}$ into $k$ clusters $\{C_1, \dots, C_k\}$ by minimizing the inter-cluster edge cut:
    $$ \min \sum_{i=1}^k \mathrm{cut}(C_i, \mathcal{V} \setminus C_i) $$
    Edge weights for the cut will be defined by the number of RANSAC inliers to preserve strong connections within clusters.
2.  **Processing:** Each cluster is independently converted to a line graph and processed by the GNN.
3.  **Aggregation:** Since an edge from $\mathcal{G}$ may appear in multiple clusters (boundary edges), we will aggregate predictions using **majority voting** to produce the final classification.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Framework Reformulation:** We provide a novel formulation of SfM outlier rejection by mapping the edge-filtering problem in the spatial domain to a vertex-classification problem in the line-graph domain.
2.  **Structural Robustness:** By utilizing a Transformer-based GNN, we expect to capture high-order structural dependencies that simple geometric checks (like loop consistency) miss.
3.  **Scalability:** The proposed clustering-based inference mechanism will allow complex line-graph operations to be applied to large-scale, real-world reconstruction problems without hitting memory bottlenecks.
4.  **Integration:** The system is designed as a modular pre-processing step that can be seamlessly inserted into any global SfM pipeline (e.g., Theia, GLOMAP) prior to translation averaging.

notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.

preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
